Miscompilation with FFI `bool` return type on AArch64 *[View all comments](https://triagebot.infra.rust-lang.org/gh-comments/rust-lang/rust/issues/159244)* I tried this C and Rust code: ```c struct Bools { _Bool a; _Bool b; }; _Bool get_a(struct Bools bools) { return bools.a; } ``` ```rust #[repr(C)] struct Bools { a: bool, b: bool, } #[link(name = "get_a")] unsafe extern "C" { safe fn get_a(bools: Bools) -> bool; } pub fn broken() -> i32 { let bools = Bools { a: false, b: true }; if get_a(bools) { 123 } else { 321 } } pub fn main() { if broken() == 123 { unreachable!(); } } ``` with `gcc -c get_a.c -o get_a.o -O1 && ar rcs libget_a.a get_a.o && rustc main.rs -L . -C opt-level=1 && ./main`. I expected to see this happen: clean program exit, because the value of `a` should get round-tripped and `broken` should return `321`. Instead, this happened: ``` thread 'main' (17324) panicked at main.rs:23:9: internal error: entered unreachable code ``` This is caused by `rustc` emitting the `bool` return type as `i1 zeroext` to LLVM, but that is incorrect, because the AArch64 call ABI does not guarantee that the unused bits of the register are zeroed (["any unused bits in the register have unspecified value"](https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/4374257ab4c35c91a91f8dfa71ce0c824e188cec/aapcs64/aapcs64.rst?plain=1#L2013)). `bools` is passed in a single register. The `get_a` function is a single `ret` instruction and doesn't touch the registers at all. The `if` gets turned into a `cmp w0, #0` which compares the lower 32 bits of register, including the value of `b`, to `0`. This is similar to https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/97463 which was fixed in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/97800, but only covered integer types. I originally encountered this as spurious Java exception because the `jni-rs` [ExceptionCheck](https://github.com/jni-rs/jni-sys/blob/809b4c4939a2a581b84aa17018a5033b71c6d435/jni-sys/src/lib.rs#L1292) has a [`bool`](https://github.com/jni-rs/jni-sys/blob/809b4c4939a2a581b84aa17018a5033b71c6d435/jni-sys/src/lib.rs#L17) return type. ### LLM disclosure I used LLMs to help find the cause of my initial issue, and discover resources for areas I wasn't familiar enough with (rustc internals, JNI, LLVM, AArch64 calling convention). Performance regression since 1.93 related to MaybeUninit being wrongfully initialized

Since rustc 1.93 (likely #147827), initializing newtype wrapper of a struct that contains an integer type and a MaybeUninit field generates code to initialize the entire struct at -O2, instead of writing only the initialized integer field.

First bad nightly: nightly-2025-11-24 (commit c23ed3ef28b)
Last good nightly: nightly-2025-11-23 (commit 94b49fd99)
Still broken as of: 1.98.0-nightly (2026-06-11, LLVM 22.1.6)

Real-world impact: this caused a 22% performance regression in a specific test in the Firefox performance suite, as reported in https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2046376.
The hot call site creates a struct of three empty SmallVecs (from the smallvec crate with the union feature enabled). With rustc 1.93 the hot path now calls memset for 1224-bytes instead of three 8-byte stores.

### Minimal reproducer

```rust
use std::mem::MaybeUninit;

pub struct Vec { cap: usize, data: MaybeUninit<[u64; 2]> }
pub struct Wrap(Vec);

#[no_mangle]
#[inline(never)]
pub fn make() -> Wrap {
    Wrap(Vec { cap: 0, data: MaybeUninit::uninit() })
}
```
https://godbolt.org/z/KnarEEon8

1.92 generates:
```
make:
        movq    %rdi, %rax
        movq    $0, 16(%rdi)
        retq
```

1.93 generates:
```
make:
        movq    %rdi, %rax
        xorps   %xmm0, %xmm0
        movups  %xmm0, (%rdi)
        movq    $0, 16(%rdi)
        retq
```

With larger arrays in the MaybeUninit, more movups happen, up to the point where it may choose to use memset instead.
IOW, 19.3 is initializing the whole struct instead. Without the wrapping, the MaybeUninit is properly not initialized.

Mishandling of AAPCS64 Homogeneous Vector Aggregates (HVAs) on aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu I tried this code: https://rust.godbolt.org/z/EdrsY7517 I expected to see this happen: C code and `extern "C"` + `#[repr(C)]` Rust code with identical code and types to have identical-ish output. Instead, this happened: I've been debugging performance issues related to returning multiple values from a function and noticed that aggregates of `u64` were not producing expected machine code. With the help of LLM I discovered what looks like AAPCS64 HVA violation. Interestingly, floats (HFA) work as expected.
LLM-generated description comparing C and Rust side by side ## Summary On `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `extern "C"` functions that return (or take by value) a `#[repr(C)]` struct or array composed of 1-4 identical NEON "short vector" members (e.g. `float64x2_t`, `uint64x1_t`) are lowered using the indirect-result convention: the aggregate is written to memory pointed to by `x8` (for returns) or read from a pointer passed in `x0` (for arguments), instead of being passed/returned directly in `v0`-`v3`. Per AAPCS64 §5.4.2 ("Homogeneous Aggregates"), such an aggregate is a Homogeneous Vector Aggregate (HVA) and must use the vector register file exactly like a Homogeneous Floating-point Aggregate (HFA) of `f32`/`f64` does — and rustc does implement that HFA case correctly (see the `ThreeF64` control case below). Only the vector-member (HVA) case is wrong. GCC, targeting the same platform ABI, keeps every one of these values in `v`/`d` registers with no spill to memory, confirming the expected behaviour. ## Cases and results ### Case 1 — `struct { float64x2_t a, b; }` (32 bytes, 2 members) ```rust #[repr(C)] pub struct TwoF64x2 { pub a: float64x2_t, pub b: float64x2_t } pub extern "C" fn ret_two_f64x2() -> TwoF64x2 { .. } pub extern "C" fn arg_two_f64x2(x: TwoF64x2) -> float64x2_t { .. } ``` **Expected (AAPCS64 HVA):** returned in `v0`-`v1`; argument passed in `v0`-`v1`. **Actual (rustc):** ```asm ret_two_f64x2: fmov v0.2d, #1.00000000 fmov v1.2d, #2.00000000 stp q0, q1, [x8] ; <-- spilled to memory via indirect-result pointer x8 ret arg_two_f64x2: ldp q0, q1, [x0] ; <-- argument read back from memory via pointer x0 fadd v0.2d, v0.2d, v1.2d ret ``` Both directions are wrong: the return value is written through `x8` instead of being left in `v0`/`v1`, and the argument is received as a pointer in `x0` and loaded from memory instead of arriving directly in `v0`/`v1`. ### Case 2 — `struct { uint64x1_t a, b, c; }` (24 bytes, 3 members) ```rust #[repr(C)] pub struct ThreeU64x1 { pub a: uint64x1_t, pub b: uint64x1_t, pub c: uint64x1_t } pub extern "C" fn ret_three_u64x1() -> ThreeU64x1 { .. } pub extern "C" fn arg_three_u64x1(x: ThreeU64x1) -> uint64x1_t { .. } ``` **Expected (AAPCS64 HVA):** returned in `v0`-`v2` (as `d0`-`d2`, since these are 8-byte vectors); argument passed the same way. **Actual (rustc):** ```asm ret_three_u64x1: mov w9, #1 mov w10, #2 fmov d0, x9 fmov d1, x10 mov w9, #3 stp d0, d1, [x8] ; <-- spilled to memory via x8 fmov d0, x9 str d0, [x8, #16] ; <-- spilled to memory via x8 ret arg_three_u64x1: ldr d0, [x0] ; <-- argument read back from memory via pointer x0 ret ``` Same defect: values are computed in `d` registers and then immediately stored out through `x8`/`x0` instead of being kept in registers for the caller. ### Case 3 (control) — `struct { f64 a, b, c; }` (24 bytes, HFA of scalars) ```rust #[repr(C)] pub struct ThreeF64 { pub a: f64, pub b: f64, pub c: f64 } pub extern "C" fn ret_three_f64() -> ThreeF64 { .. } ``` **This works correctly today:** ```asm ret_three_f64: fmov d0, #1.00000000 fmov d1, #2.00000000 fmov d2, #3.00000000 ret ``` No `x8`, no memory traffic — the values are left directly in `d0`-`d2`. This shows the HFA register-return path is implemented; it is specifically the HVA (vector member) case that is missing the equivalent handling. ### Case 4a — array form: `[uint64x2_t; 2]` (32 bytes, 2 elements) AAPCS64 HVA rules apply equally to an array of a homogeneous short-vector element type, not just to a struct. ```rust #[repr(C)] pub struct ArrayU64x2 { pub arr: [uint64x2_t; 2] } pub extern "C" fn ret_array_u64x2() -> ArrayU64x2 { .. } ``` **Expected:** returned in `v0`-`v1`. **Actual:** ```asm ret_array_u64x2: mov w9, #1 mov w10, #2 dup v0.2d, x9 dup v1.2d, x10 stp q0, q1, [x8] ; <-- spilled to memory via x8 ret ``` Same defect as the struct cases — the array form is affected too. ### Case 4b (boundary control) — `repr(transparent)` newtype around a single vector ```rust #[repr(transparent)] pub struct OneU64x2(pub uint64x2_t); pub extern "C" fn ret_one_u64x2() -> OneU64x2 { .. } ``` **This works correctly** (a single 16-byte vector trivially fits in `v0` regardless of HVA classification): ```asm ret_one_u64x2: mov w8, #42 dup v0.2d, x8 ret ``` No memory traffic. This pinpoints the boundary precisely: a bare vector, or a `repr(transparent)` wrapper around exactly one, is handled correctly; as soon as an aggregate has 2 or more homogeneous vector members (struct or array), rustc falls back to the indirect/memory convention instead of applying the HVA rule. ## Arguments vs. return values Both are affected. `arg_two_f64x2` and `arg_three_u64x1` above show the argument being received as a pointer (`x0`) and loaded from memory, rather than arriving directly in `v0`-`v2`, mirroring the return-value bug. ## What GCC does for the equivalent C (ground truth for the ABI) ``` $ aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc -O2 -S repro.c -o repro-gcc.s ``` `repro.c` (attached) defines the same aggregates via ``. GCC's output for the two-vector-struct case: ```asm ret_two_f64x2_c: adrp x0, .LC0 ldr q0, [x0, #:lo12:.LC0] adrp x0, .LC1 ldr q1, [x0, #:lo12:.LC1] ret ; result entirely in v0/v1, no x8 involved arg_two_f64x2_c: fadd v0.2d, v1.2d, v0.2d ret ; argument arrives directly in v0/v1 ``` and for the three-`uint64x1_t`-struct case: ```asm ret_three_u64x1_c: adrp x0, .LC2 ldr d0, [x0, #:lo12:.LC2] adrp x0, .LC3 ldr d1, [x0, #:lo12:.LC3] adrp x0, .LC4 ldr d2, [x0, #:lo12:.LC4] ret ; result entirely in d0/d1/d2, no x8 involved arg_three_u64x1_c: ret ; argument's value (x.a) is already in d0, a no-op return ``` and for the array case: ```asm ret_array_u64x2_c: adrp x0, .LC6 ldr q0, [x0, #:lo12:.LC6] adrp x0, .LC7 ldr q1, [x0, #:lo12:.LC7] ret ; result entirely in v0/v1, no x8 involved ``` In every case GCC keeps the whole aggregate in `v`/`d` registers with zero use of `x8` or a memory round trip — confirming that per the platform ABI these types are HVAs and must be register-passed, and that rustc's current codegen (which spills through `x8`/reads through a pointer argument) does not conform. ## Expected behaviour per AAPCS64 AAPCS64 §5.4.2 defines an aggregate as "homogeneous" if it has at most 4 members (or array elements) that are all the same fundamental type, which may be a floating-point type (HFA) or a "short vector type" — an 8-byte or 16-byte NEON vector such as `float64x2_t`/`uint64x1_t`/`uint64x2_t` (HVA). Per §6.4.2/§6.8.2, an HVA result/argument is passed using the NSAA/NGRN-analogous vector rules: allocated one `v` register per member (`v0`-`v3` for return, `v0`-`v7` for arguments), not passed via the indirect-result register `x8` or via a pointer, and not counted against the general-purpose "large aggregate passed by reference" fallback. This applies identically whether the homogeneous members come from a `struct` or from an array. rustc currently applies this correctly for HFAs (scalar `f32`/`f64` members) but not for HVAs (NEON vector members), for both struct and array aggregates, and for both argument and return-value positions.
